title: Lesson 11 - A2.1.4-5 Operating Systems and Mobile Devices (Independent Study)
subject: Information Technology
bigQuestion: How do unsupported devices create security risks?

sections.heading: Operating system vulnerabilities
sections.text: An operating system (OS) is the system software that runs a device: it manages the hardware and lets apps run. An OS vulnerability is a weakness in an OS that could be exploited by an attacker, especially when the OS is unsupported, unpatched or poorly secured.
points: Example: an old OS reaches end-of-life and no longer gets security patches, leaving known vulnerabilities unfixed
Application: enable automatic updates, keep anti-malware and firewalls switched on, and upgrade or replace devices when the OS becomes unsupported

sections.heading: Why operating systems become a risk
points: An OS can be used for many years, especially on desktop PCs
Both GUI (graphical, point-and-click) and CLI (command line, typed commands) systems need regular updates to fix security problems
End-of-life: the manufacturer stops supporting the OS and stops providing security updates
People delay upgrading because of cost, compatibility issues or older hardware
To stay secure: enable automatic updates, and switch on anti-malware and firewall settings
If vulnerabilities aren't fixed through updates and patches, attackers can damage systems, steal data or spread malware

head: Attack
Vulnerability
What happened and impact
Lesson
rows: Blaster worm (2003)
Weakness in Windows XP/2000
Spread between vulnerable computers, causing crashes and restarts. Millions infected
Install security patches and use firewalls
Conficker (2008)
Weakness in the Windows Server service
Spread across networks and built a large botnet. Millions infected
Use patches, antivirus and network security
WannaCry (2017)
Weakness in Windows' SMB network service
Ransomware spread across networks without anyone opening a file. Over 200,000 computers, including the NHS
Install security updates as soon as possible
Spectre and Meltdown (2018)
Weaknesses in computer processors, not the OS itself
Attackers could potentially read data in memory. Affected many modern computers
Security problems can exist in hardware as well as software

sections.heading: Mobile devices and OEM updates
sections.text: Mobile devices run an operating system such as Android or iOS. Apps often update automatically, but system updates depend on the OEM (original equipment manufacturer, i.e. the device maker) releasing them.
points: If an OEM is slow to release an update, the device stays vulnerable to known threats
Google or Apple may create the security fix, but the phone manufacturer and network provider may need to approve and release it first
Older devices may stop getting updates completely, leaving vulnerabilities unpatched
Key point: a phone can work perfectly normally but still be vulnerable if its manufacturer no longer provides security updates

head: Stage
What happens
rows: 1. Device release
The device is launched and becomes available to users
2. Active updates
The manufacturer provides regular OS and security updates to keep it secure
3. End-of-support
Updates stop. The device still works, but new vulnerabilities are no longer fixed
4. Potential risks
Without security updates, it becomes more and more vulnerable to malware, hacking and other threats

diagram.alt: Four stages in order: Release, when the device is launched; Active updates, when the manufacturer sends regular OS and security updates; End-of-support, when updates stop but the phone still works; and Rising risk, when known flaws are never fixed. A bar underneath shows security risk staying low while patched, then rising sharply after end-of-support.
diagram.caption: A phone can keep working after end-of-support, but its risk keeps rising.

sections.heading: Reducing the risk of unsupported devices
sections.text: From the slides, plus standard measures (marked *) to use in exam answers:
points: Upgrade or replace devices when the OS or phone becomes unsupported
Enable automatic updates for as long as updates are available
Keep anti-malware and firewalls switched on
* Check a device's update policy (how many years of support) before buying, and plan replacements
* Stop unsupported devices accessing sensitive data or the main network until they're replaced
* Use mobile device management (MDM) software to track which devices are out of support

keyIdea: Devices stay safe only while they get security updates. When an operating system or phone reaches end-of-life, or its OEM is slow to release fixes, known vulnerabilities stay open, as Blaster, Conficker and WannaCry showed. So update automatically and replace unsupported devices.
flashcards: Operating system (OS)
System software that manages a device's hardware and lets applications run, e.g. Windows, Android, iOS.
OS vulnerability
A weakness in an OS that could be exploited, especially when it is unsupported, unpatched or poorly secured.
End-of-life (EOL)
When the manufacturer stops supporting an OS or device and stops providing security updates.
Unsupported OS
An operating system that no longer receives security updates, so known vulnerabilities stay unfixed.
GUI
Graphical user interface: point-and-click windows and icons. Needs regular updates like any OS.
CLI
Command line interface: users type commands. Also needs regular updates.
Why people delay upgrading
Cost, compatibility issues and older hardware.
Staying secure (OS)
Enable automatic updates; keep anti-malware and firewall switched on; upgrade when unsupported.
Blaster worm (2003)
Exploited a Windows XP/2000 weakness, caused crashes and restarts, infected millions. Lesson: patch and use firewalls.
Conficker (2008)
Exploited the Windows Server service and built a large botnet. Lesson: patches, antivirus, network security.
WannaCry (2017)
Ransomware exploiting Windows' SMB service; spread without opening a file; 200,000+ computers including the NHS.
SMB
A Windows network service for sharing files. Its weakness was exploited by WannaCry.
Spectre and Meltdown (2018)
Processor (hardware) weaknesses that could let attackers read data in memory.
OEM
Original equipment manufacturer: the company that makes the device and releases its system updates.
Why OEMs matter
They release system updates; if they're slow or stop, devices stay vulnerable.
Update chain (mobile)
Google/Apple create the fix → the phone maker and network provider approve and release it.
Mobile device lifecycle
Device release → active updates → end-of-support → growing risks.
End-of-support device
Still works normally, but no longer gets fixes for new vulnerabilities.
Mobile device management (MDM)
Software organisations use to manage and track their phones and tablets (standard term).

o: Updates fix security weaknesses, so attackers can't exploit them

quiz.q: What is an unsupported operating system?
o: One that no longer receives security updates from the manufacturer
quiz.e: After end-of-life, known vulnerabilities stay unfixed.

quiz.q: Why might people delay upgrading their OS?
o: Cost, compatibility issues or older hardware
Upgrades are always free and easy
quiz.e: These are the three reasons on the slides.
The OEM is the device maker, responsible for releasing system updates.

quiz.q: Why are OEMs important for mobile device security?
o: They release system updates; if they're slow or stop, the device stays vulnerable
quiz.e: Apps update themselves, but OS updates depend on the OEM.

quiz.q: A phone works perfectly but no longer gets security updates. Is it secure?
o: No, new vulnerabilities won't be fixed

quiz.q: Which attack spread through a weakness in Windows' SMB service without users opening a file?
quiz.e: WannaCry (2017) hit over 200,000 computers, including the NHS.

quiz.q: What made Spectre and Meltdown different from the other examples?

What comes straight after 'Active updates' in a mobile device's lifecycle?

apply.title: Supported or at risk?
apply.intro: Decide what the risk is, or what should be done, in each situation.

items.task: A school still uses PCs running an operating system that reached end-of-life three years ago.
o: Completely safe, as it still works
Unsupported OS: known vulnerabilities stay unfixed
items.e: No more security patches, so known vulnerabilities stay open. Upgrade or replace.

items.task: A shop delays upgrading its till PCs because its old card machine software won't work on the new OS. Which reason is this?
items.e: Compatibility problems are a common reason for delaying upgrades, and they leave systems exposed.

items.task: Google releases an Android security fix, but a particular phone brand takes months to send it to users.
o: The phones are now fully secure
Slow OEM update: the phones stay vulnerable
items.e: Fixes depend on the OEM releasing them.

items.task: Ransomware spreads across a hospital network through an unpatched Windows network service, without anyone opening a file.
o: Like WannaCry: install security updates ASAP
items.e: WannaCry exploited unpatched SMB. The patch was the fix.

items.task: A worker's 6-year-old phone still makes calls and runs apps, but the maker stopped updates two years ago. Should it access company email?
o: No, it's past end-of-support and vulnerable
items.e: A working phone can still be insecure if it no longer gets updates.

items.task: Researchers find a flaw in computer processors that could let attackers read data in memory.
o: Hardware vulnerability, like Spectre and Meltdown
items.e: Security problems can exist in hardware as well as software.

items.task: Which setting should be switched on to keep an OS secure?
items.e: Automatic updates, plus anti-malware and firewall.

items.task: A worm spreads between unpatched Windows XP computers, making them crash and restart.
o: Like Blaster: patch and use firewalls

items.task: A company is choosing new phones for staff. What should it check, security-wise?
o: How many years of security updates the OEM promises
items.e: Update policies differ between makers, as in the wider reading.

items.task: A device has just been launched, and the maker sends regular OS and security updates. Which lifecycle stage is this?
items.e: During active updates the device is kept secure.

items.task: Malware spreads across a network and turns infected computers into a huge botnet using a Windows Server weakness.
A company can't replace its unsupported phones until next year. What's the best way to reduce the risk until then?
o: Limit their access to sensitive data and keep anti-malware on
items.e: Reduce what an unsupported device can reach, and keep other protections on, until it's replaced.

pts: System software that manages a device's hardware and resources
and lets applications run and users interact with the device (e.g. Windows, Android, iOS)
exam.tip: What it is + what it does, with an example.

exam.q: 2. What is an unsupported operating system?
pts: An operating system that has reached end-of-life, so the manufacturer no longer supports it
and no longer provides security updates, so known vulnerabilities stay unfixed
exam.tip: End-of-life + no security updates + the consequence.

exam.q: 3. Explain why it is important to keep an operating system updated.
pts: Updates and patches fix known security weaknesses in the OS
so attackers can't exploit them to damage systems, steal data or spread malware
exam.tip: Point + linked consequence. You could use WannaCry as evidence.

exam.q: 4. Explain why OEMs are important for mobile device security.
pts: System (OS) updates for mobile devices depend on the OEM (the device manufacturer) releasing them
If the OEM is slow, or fixes from Google/Apple must be approved by the OEM and network provider first, the device stays vulnerable for longer
When the OEM stops updates (end-of-support), vulnerabilities are never fixed, even though the phone still works
exam.tip: Who releases updates → what happens if they're slow → what happens when they stop.

exam.q: 5. Give two ways an organisation can reduce the risks of unsupported devices.
pts: Any one: upgrade or replace unsupported devices
A second: enable automatic updates / keep anti-malware and firewalls on / restrict unsupported devices' access to sensitive data

exam.q: 6. Describe the lifecycle of a mobile device.
pts: Device release: launched and available to users
Active updates: the manufacturer provides regular OS and security updates
End-of-support: updates stop, but the device can still work
Potential risks: without updates it becomes more and more vulnerable to malware and hacking
exam.tip: One mark per stage, in order.

exam.q: 7. Using the WannaCry attack as an example, explain how an unpatched operating system vulnerability can be exploited.
pts: WannaCry exploited a weakness in Windows' SMB network service
Computers without the security update were vulnerable, and the ransomware spread across networks without anyone opening a file
Over 200,000 computers were affected, including NHS systems, which shows why updates must be installed quickly
exam.tip: Vulnerability → how it spread → impact → lesson.

exam.sc: A company has 50 smartphones that are no longer receiving security updates from the manufacturer.
exam.q: 8. Explain the security risks to the company and suggest ways these risks could be reduced.
pts: Risk: new vulnerabilities in the phones' OS will no longer be patched, so known weaknesses stay open
Risk: attackers could exploit them to install malware or spyware, or take control of the phones
Impact: company data on the phones (emails, files, passwords) could be stolen, and an infected phone could be a route into the company network
Scale: with 50 phones, there are many weak points, and one compromised phone is enough
Reduce: replace or upgrade the phones with models that still get updates, and check the OEM's update policy before buying
Reduce (until replaced): restrict the phones' access to sensitive data and the network, keep anti-malware on, and install any remaining updates
exam.tip: This is the slides' own exam question. Top marks need risks AND impacts AND realistic solutions, all linked to the 50 phones.
